title: Mobile broadband 4G/5G
desc: Internet over the mobile network: SIMs, 5G, antennas, failover

pages.t: Mobile broadband is internet delivered over the same cellular network your phone uses. A cellular router takes a SIM card and shares that connection with laptops, cameras and machines over Ethernet or Wi-Fi.
g: Cellular router
A router that gets its internet from a SIM card and the mobile network instead of a cable.
SIM
The small card (or chip) that identifies a subscription on the mobile network.

pages.t: Mobile networks come in generations. 4G (also called LTE) is what most people use today. 5G is the newer generation. Older 3G and 2G exist as a fallback in many routers.
g: LTE
Long Term Evolution: the technology behind 4G.
3G / 2G
Older generations, slower, used as a fallback.

pages.t: Cellular is the answer when a cable is too slow to install, too expensive, or not possible: temporary sites, remote buildings and vehicles. It is also a popular backup when the main fixed line fails.
g: Backup
A second connection that takes over when the main one fails.

quiz.q: What does a cellular router need to get online?
quiz.w: It gets internet from the mobile network through a SIM.

quiz.q: Which is another name for 4G?
quiz.w: LTE is the technology behind 4G.
g: ADSL
An older internet service over telephone copper lines.

quiz.q: A customer needs internet at a temporary event site in two days. Best idea?
o: A cellular router with a data SIM
quiz.w: Cellular is fast to deploy where a cable would take too long.

pages.t: A SIM holds the identity and secret key that prove to the network who you are and which subscription you pay for. Common sizes are mini, micro and nano, the smallest removable one, used in phones.
g: Nano-SIM
The small SIM size used in most modern phones and many routers.

pages.t: An eSIM is a chip built into the device. It cannot be removed, but its subscription can be changed remotely by software. A device can hold several profiles, with one or two active at a time.
g: eSIM
A SIM built into the device, programmed over the air.
Profile
One stored subscription on an eSIM.

pages.t: eSIM suits devices that are sealed or hard to reach, and large IoT roll-outs, since nobody needs to swap cards. A normal SIM slot is still more flexible for small projects. Always check whether the product supports the type the customer wants.
g: IoT
Internet of Things: devices like meters and sensors that connect on their own.

quiz.q: How is an eSIM different from a normal SIM?
o: It is built in and can be reprogrammed remotely
quiz.w: An eSIM is an embedded chip whose subscription is set up over the air.

quiz.q: Where is eSIM especially useful?
quiz.w: Not having to swap a card is valuable when devices are sealed or numerous.

quiz.q: A customer wants to change operator in the field with no tools. What helps?
quiz.w: eSIM profiles can be changed by software, and dual SIM slots allow switching between two subscriptions.

pages.t: 5G is not just faster. It aims at three things: faster mobile broadband, very reliable low-delay connections for critical uses, and massive IoT with huge numbers of devices. Many customers will mostly notice speed and response time.
g: Latency
The delay before data starts to flow. Lower is better for real-time use.

pages.t: Low-band 5G reaches far and goes through walls but is slower. Mid-band is the compromise. High-band, mmWave, is very fast but reaches only short distances and is blocked easily by walls. Higher frequency: faster but shorter range.
g: mmWave
Very high frequency 5G: huge speed, tiny range.
Band
A slice of radio frequencies used for mobile service.

pages.t: Not always. If 4G coverage is good, 4G is cheaper and plenty for cameras, POS and backup. Choose 5G when the site needs more speed, when the area has good 5G coverage, or when the project must last for years.
g: POS
Point of sale: the till or card terminal in a shop.

quiz.q: Which 5G type reaches farthest and enters buildings best?
quiz.w: Lower frequencies travel farther and pass through walls better, at lower speed.

quiz.q: What is the catch with mmWave?
o: Very short range and easily blocked
quiz.w: High frequencies give big speed but lose strength quickly through obstacles.

quiz.q: A shop only needs a backup line for a card terminal. Which is the sensible starting point?
o: A 4G router, if 4G coverage is good
quiz.w: A card terminal uses little data, so 4G is usually enough and cheaper.

pages.t: Non-standalone (NSA) adds 5G radio on top of the existing 4G core. Standalone (SA) uses a brand-new 5G core. Early rollouts were NSA, because operators could add 5G without replacing the core.
g: Core network
The operator's central systems that handle subscribers, sessions and data.
NSA
Non-standalone: 5G radio relying on the 4G core.
SA
Standalone: 5G radio with its own 5G core.

pages.t: With NSA, users get 5G radio benefits such as lower delay, but only 4G services. Only SA supports the full set of 5G services, such as network slicing, separate virtual networks for different needs.
g: Network slicing
Running several separate virtual networks over one physical network.

pages.t: A router must support the mode the operator uses. A 5G router that supports NSA only may miss out on SA features, and the other way round. Ask which operator, and whether it offers SA in the area.
g: Operator
The mobile network company, such as Telia or Elisa.

quiz.q: What does NSA 5G rely on?
quiz.w: Non-standalone adds 5G radio to the 4G core network.

quiz.q: Which mode supports the full set of 5G services?
quiz.w: Only standalone offers all 5G phase 1 services.

quiz.q: A customer wants network slicing. What do you check?
o: Whether the operator offers SA and the router supports it
quiz.w: Slicing needs a standalone 5G network and compatible equipment.

pages.t: A band is a slice of radio spectrum. Operators use different bands in different countries, so a router must support the bands your operator uses. A device from one region may not work well in another.
g: Spectrum
The range of radio frequencies available for use.

pages.t: Carrier aggregation joins several frequency blocks into one connection for a user. More blocks means a higher peak speed and better use of the network. It can combine blocks in the same band or in different bands.
g: Carrier aggregation (CA)
Combining several channels so one device gets more total speed.

pages.t: Carrier aggregation is a spec-sheet line that tells you the router can use it if the operator offers it. It is only a benefit where the network supports it. Do not promise speeds, but ask about coverage and the operator.
g: Peak speed
The theoretical top speed in ideal conditions, rarely what you get all the time.

quiz.q: What is carrier aggregation?
o: Combining several frequency blocks for one connection
Sharing a SIM between two routers
quiz.w: It joins component carriers so a device can get more speed.

quiz.q: Why must a router support the right bands?
o: Operators use specific bands, and the router must be able to use them
quiz.w: If the router lacks the operator's bands, coverage or speed suffers.

quiz.q: A customer asks for a guaranteed speed because the router lists carrier aggregation. Reply?
o: It can help where the operator supports it, but speeds vary
quiz.w: Peak speeds are theoretical and depend on the network.

pages.t: An LTE category, like Cat 4, tells you what a device's modem can do at most. Peak rates depend on the user equipment category. A higher category number generally means a higher possible speed.
g: Modem
The part that talks to the mobile network.
Cat (category)
A class number describing a modem's capability, such as Cat 4.

pages.t: The category is a ceiling, not what the user will get. Real speed depends on signal, congestion and the operator. Two routers with the same category can behave differently in a weak signal area, where the antennas matter.
g: Congestion
Too many users sharing the same cell, which slows everyone.

pages.t: Cat 4 is a sensible choice for cameras, backup lines and IoT. For many users or heavy use, look at higher categories or 5G. Match the category to the workload, not to the biggest number on the box.
g: Workload
What the customer will actually do with the connection.

quiz.q: What does an LTE category describe?
o: The maximum capability of the modem
quiz.w: It is a capability class that sets a ceiling on peak speed.

quiz.q: Does Cat 6 guarantee better speed than Cat 4 in every case?
o: No, it is only a ceiling and real speed depends on signal and congestion
quiz.w: Real-world speed depends on the network and signal.

quiz.q: A shop needs a backup line for a till and a camera. Which is likely enough?
o: A modest category such as Cat 4
quiz.w: Light workloads rarely need the highest category.

pages.t: A mobile signal reaches a router by several bounced paths, which can cancel each other out. With two or more antennas, one antenna often still gets a good signal when another is in a dead spot. That is why many routers have two.
g: Diversity
Using multiple antennas so the receiver picks the best signal.
MIMO
Multiple antennas at both ends to send and receive more data at once.

pages.t: External antennas can be moved or replaced. A better or outdoor antenna on a cable can sit near a window or on a roof, where the signal is stronger, while the router stays indoors. This often fixes a weak-signal site cheaply.
g: Window
Glass and walls weaken the signal, so being near a window or outside helps.

pages.t: Place the router or antenna high and near a window, away from metal and thick walls. If the signal is weak inside a building, an external antenna or an outdoor unit is the first thing to suggest, before blaming the router.
g: Signal strength
How strong the received signal is, shown in bars or in dBm.

quiz.q: Why do routers often have two antennas?
o: If one antenna is in a dead spot, the other often still gets a signal
quiz.w: Different antennas see different interference, so diversity improves reliability.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of an external antenna on a cable?
o: It makes the router faster by itself
It can be placed where the signal is strongest
quiz.w: It lets the antenna sit at a better spot than the router.

quiz.q: A cottage has weak signal indoors. First suggestion?
o: Move the antenna higher or outdoors, or use external antennas
quiz.w: Better antenna placement often fixes weak signal cheaply.

lessons.title: Indoor vs outdoor units and FWA

pages.t: Indoor routers sit in a room, powered from a socket, and are the simple choice where signal is good. They are cheap and easy, but walls cost signal, so reception depends on the building.
g: Indoor unit
A router designed to live inside, protected from weather.

pages.t: Outdoor units mount on a wall or mast, often powered by PoE, and are built for weather. They stand where the signal is best and connect to the building by cable. They suit remote houses, cottages and farms.
g: PoE
Power over Ethernet: power and data on one network cable.
Mast
A pole used to mount an antenna or unit high up.

pages.t: FWA delivers home or business broadband over a radio link instead of a cable. Using 5G or 4G, it is especially useful in rural areas where laying cable is expensive. It is often the main line, not just a backup.
g: FWA
Fixed wireless access: broadband over a radio link to a fixed location.

quiz.q: Which unit type suits a remote farmhouse with weak signal?
o: Outdoor unit on a wall or mast
quiz.w: An outdoor unit can stand where the signal is best.

quiz.q: What does FWA stand for?
quiz.w: FWA is broadband delivered by radio to a fixed location.

quiz.q: Why are outdoor units often powered by PoE?
o: It removes the need for a SIM
One cable brings both power and data to the mast
quiz.w: PoE avoids a separate power cable out to the unit.

pages.t: WAN failover means a router switches to a backup connection when the main one fails. Dual SIM means two SIM slots, so it can switch to a second operator if the first has no signal.
g: WAN
Wide area network: the connection to the internet outside your building.
Failover
Automatically switching to a backup when the main connection fails.

pages.t: Typical triggers on a dual SIM router include weak signal, no network, a failed data connection, a data limit reached, or roaming. The router checks and swaps to the other SIM or the other WAN.
g: Roaming
Using another operator's network, often when abroad, usually at higher cost.

pages.t: A common office setup: the fixed line is primary, cellular is the backup. When the line drops, the router moves to 4G or 5G in seconds. Shops, clinics and anything with card payments love this.
g: Primary / backup
The main connection and the one that waits in reserve.

quiz.q: What is the point of dual SIM?
o: Switch to a second operator if the first fails
Share one SIM with two people
quiz.w: Two SIMs give resilience across two networks.

quiz.q: Which can trigger a SIM switch?
o: A new colour on the box
quiz.w: Routers can switch on conditions like weak signal, no network or a failed data connection.

quiz.q: A shop has a fibre line and needs card payments to keep working. Recommend?
o: A cellular router as backup with failover
quiz.w: Cellular backup keeps payments running when the main line drops.

quiz.q: What does WAN mean in failover?
o: The connection to the outside internet
quiz.w: WAN is the connection out to the wider internet.

pages.t: Cottages and remote buildings often have no fixed line, so an outdoor 4G or 5G unit is the main internet. Building sites are temporary: a rugged cellular router can be set up in an hour and moved later.
g: Rugged
Built for dust, vibration, weather and a wide temperature range.

pages.h: On the move and the unattended
pages.t: Vehicles such as buses and service vans use cellular routers for passenger Wi-Fi and fleet data. IoT sites like meters, signs and cameras use small routers or eSIM devices that nobody visits often.
g: Fleet
A group of vehicles managed together.

pages.t: Offices, shops and clinics use cellular as a safety net. Remote management helps too: the vendor's platform lets a reseller monitor many routers from one place. Mention that it is often easier to manage than to install.
g: Remote management
Monitoring and configuring devices over the internet instead of visiting each one.

quiz.q: Which customer is a classic fit for cellular as the main internet?
o: A city office with fibre only
A cottage with no fixed line
quiz.w: Where no cable exists, mobile broadband is the practical main line.

quiz.q: Why do vehicles use cellular routers?
o: They move, so a cable is impossible
quiz.w: Moving vehicles can only connect over mobile networks.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of remote management for a reseller?
o: Watch and update many routers from one place
quiz.w: A central platform saves visits to each site.

pages.t: Start with coverage: which operator works at the site, 4G or 5G, and what is the signal like indoors? Check the operator's map, then test with a phone on site. No signal means no router will help.
g: Coverage
Whether the mobile network reaches the location with usable signal.

pages.t: Ask how much data the use needs. Cameras and video use a lot, backup uses little. Check the plan type and any limits. Then power: is there a socket, PoE, or only 12 V in a vehicle or on a mast?
g: Data plan
The subscription's monthly data allowance and price terms.

pages.t: Who manages it, how critical is uptime, is a backup SIM needed, and is the site fixed or moving? These questions point to indoor or outdoor, 4G or 5G, one SIM or two. Write the answers down before quoting.
g: Uptime
The share of time a connection is working.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to establish?
quiz.w: Without usable signal, no router can deliver.

quiz.q: Why ask about data use?
o: It decides the antenna length only
Cameras and video need far more data than a till backup
quiz.w: Plans and limits must fit the workload.

quiz.q: A customer wants a router on a mast far from any building. Which question matters most next?
o: How will it be powered, for example PoE?
quiz.w: Power at remote spots decides what hardware fits.
